frictionVectors.title: European Gas Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons and remains a key gas supplier to Europe. European diversification and pressure for competitive pricing limit its leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases surveillance and defense costs. Algiers is resisting foreign military footprints while seeking to preserve influence in the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor has attracted substantial US and European interest as an alternative route for critical minerals from the central African copperbelt. Luanda gains diplomatic leverage but must prevent foreign financing from translating into excessive control over infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt obligations and declining oil production constrain fiscal sovereignty. Chinese-linked financing remains important even as Angola diversifies partnerships toward Western investors and Gulf capital.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and complicated use of the port of Cotonou. Benin is balancing regional security commitments with the need to preserve commercial access to its hinterland.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, logistics, and energy expansion rely heavily on foreign capital and contractors. This improves connectivity but leaves strategic infrastructure exposed to creditor, operator, and geopolitical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Partnership Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with major diamond partners and is seeking greater domestic value addition. Global demand weakness and synthetic stones still threaten revenue sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, coal, and other critical minerals is increasing competition among foreign investors. Gaborone retains comparatively strong institutions but must avoid replacing diamond dependence with opaque concession structures.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Control
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pursuing greater state control over gold production and contracting while challenging established foreign mining interests. Informal mining, smuggling, and insecurity limit the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence Shift
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou has reduced reliance on French security ties and deepened cooperation with Russia and regional partners. This increases political autonomy in the short term but introduces new dependencies in arms, training, and mining diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control and local processing of nickel and rare-earth prospects, but financing, technical capacity, and opaque licensing remain constraints. External investors retain significant leverage over project development.

frictionVectors.title: Border and corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Tensions linked to eastern DRC conflict and strained relations with Rwanda complicate trade access and transport planning. Burundi remains dependent on regional corridors and neighboring ports for fuel and exports.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and renewable-energy expansion relies heavily on foreign lenders, tourism capital, and development partners. This improves connectivity but limits domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's Atlantic position creates opportunities for transshipment and offshore services while exposing it to narcotics trafficking and illegal fishing. Coast-guard capacity remains dependent on international assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive value chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and mining revenues remain vulnerable to foreign concessionaires, opaque contracting, and limited domestic processing. The state retains formal ownership but captures uneven value from strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and conflict bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: The Douala-Ndjamena corridor and northern transport routes face insecurity, congestion, and financing gaps. Anglophone conflict and instability around the Far North weaken state control and raise the cost of resource movement.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining nexus
frictionVectors.details: The government relies heavily on Russian-linked security support, while access to gold and diamonds is associated with opaque and weakly regulated commercial arrangements. This reinforces regime survival but limits transparent national control of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group control of hinterlands
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to influence mining zones, cattle routes, and transport corridors outside the capital. Poor roads and limited state presence prevent consistent enforcement of licensing and taxation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal system remains heavily dependent on oil exports and foreign operators, leaving national revenue vulnerable to price cycles, contract terms, and pipeline politics. Domestic refining and broader value addition remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Security and transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: Instability along the Libya, Sudan, and Central African Republic frontiers disrupts trade and complicates control of remote resource areas. Chad also relies on external security partnerships and neighboring-state corridors to sustain strategic connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French administration of Mayotte, constraining relations with France and complicating maritime-resource claims. The dispute also fuels domestic political pressure over migration and national unity.

frictionVectors.title: DEPENDENCE ON EXTERNAL CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic fiscal capacity leaves transport, energy, and telecommunications projects dependent on foreign donors and investors. This increases exposure to competing French, Gulf, and Chinese influence.

highlights: Eastern security crisis disrupts state control

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains central to state revenue and global energy supply chains, but foreign firms, opaque intermediaries, and infrastructure-for-minerals arrangements limit effective Congolese control. Kinshasa is seeking tougher contract terms while preserving investment flows.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CORRIDOR INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and regional tensions continue to threaten mines, roads, and border trade in North and South Kivu. External diplomatic and security involvement remains necessary but also constrains Kinshasa's room for sovereign action.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The state remains heavily reliant on oil exports, leaving public finances and strategic autonomy exposed to price cycles and international energy companies. Offshore production and revenue management are persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE-FOR-RESOURCE TIES
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction have expanded roads, rail, and public infrastructure while deepening long-term external leverage. Debt servicing and project transparency remain sensitive issues for Brazzaville.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened domestic regulation and processing ambitions, but foreign traders and global manufacturers still capture significant value from cocoa exports. Price volatility and sustainability rules abroad can constrain national policy space.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion and northern transport corridors are attracting Gulf, European, Chinese, and regional investment. Competition for logistics influence is increasing as Abidjan supports West African trade while managing spillover risks from Sahel insecurity.

highlights: Red Sea risk raises infrastructure stakes

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position beside the Bab el-Mandeb through leases to multiple foreign militaries, generating revenue but limiting strategic autonomy. Rivalry among the United States, China, France, Japan, and Gulf actors increases pressure on national alignment.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Port and rail infrastructure tied to Ethiopian trade remains vital but leaves Djibouti exposed to regional instability, commercial competition, and debt-servicing pressures. Disputes over logistics assets and external financing continue to test sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Gulf capital dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and foreign-exchange shortages are driving asset sales and reliance on IMF, Gulf, and other external financing. This supports liquidity but can reduce state control over strategic infrastructure and revenue streams.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose any Ethiopian dam-filling or operating arrangements it considers insufficiently binding. The dispute keeps water security tied to regional diplomacy and wider Red Sea competition.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields are narrowing fiscal space and increasing dependence on foreign operators, technical expertise, and new offshore investment. Falling production also heightens pressure on public spending and regime stability.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure and energy deals
frictionVectors.details: Large energy and construction projects remain vulnerable to opaque contracting and concentrated foreign influence. The government retains formal ownership, but financing and operating capacity limit effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector external dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide crucial revenue but depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and marketing channels. Limited transparency and sanctions exposure complicate the conversion of mineral wealth into broad national capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline is strategically important amid regional naval competition and conflict around the Red Sea. External security interests increase the country's bargaining value while also exposing it to pressure from Gulf, Middle Eastern, and wider international actors.

highlights: Sugar and textiles face external shocks

frictionVectors.title: South African economic concentration
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport corridors, electricity links, and investment remain closely tied to South Africa. This provides stability but leaves Eswatini exposed to Pretoria's economic conditions and regional policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Preferential-market vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and apparel exports depend on preferential access to regional and Western markets. Changes in trade rules, labor standards, or subsidies could quickly affect employment and foreign-exchange earnings.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy and GERD tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam increases Addis Ababa's leverage over power generation and regional water politics. Egypt and Sudan remain concerned about operating rules, drought management, and the absence of a fully accepted binding framework.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, debt, and regional corridors
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's landlocked status drives intensive competition over access through Djibouti and other Red Sea corridors. Debt restructuring and infrastructure financing give China, Gulf states, Turkey, and neighboring governments leverage over transport and energy priorities.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain fiscally decisive

frictionVectors.title: French commercial footprint
frictionVectors.details: The new civilian government is seeking greater domestic control over oil, mining, and strategic services while renegotiating the legacy French economic presence. Paris retains influence through companies, finance, and established commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Transgabon railway vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The railway is essential for manganese exports and national connectivity, but aging infrastructure and dependence on external capital constrain Gabon's bargaining power over mineral logistics.

highlights: Fisheries and trade routes under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity allows foreign fleets to capture significant value from Gambian waters, limiting food security and state revenue. Enforcement assistance remains dependent on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal-linked corridors, border arrangements, and regional infrastructure for trade and energy access. Disruptions or political tensions can quickly raise costs for the land-constrained economy.

highlights: Gold remains the sovereign bargaining chip

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and gold leakage
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated mining damages farmland and water systems while diverting gold revenues from the formal economy. Foreign-linked supply chains and domestic political patronage complicate enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local processing and value capture in lithium, bauxite, and gold, but financing needs and debt restructuring limit its leverage with Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor control
frictionVectors.details: The rail-and-port system for Simandou iron ore gives foreign consortia substantial influence over Guinea's export architecture. The state is gaining revenue and infrastructure, but remains exposed to project financing, timelines, and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite contract imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains one of the world's major bauxite suppliers while processing capacity and local industrial linkages remain limited. Contract reviews and local-content demands risk friction with Chinese and other foreign mining interests.

highlights: Weak state control of maritime assets

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Limited maritime surveillance leaves Guinea-Bissau vulnerable to underreported catches and unfavorable access arrangements. External fleets capture much of the value from national waters while enforcement depends on foreign support.

frictionVectors.title: Port and cashew-chain influence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends on externally financed port logistics and foreign buyers for its cashew trade. This leaves producers and the state exposed to price-setting power, opaque intermediaries, and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Service Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external debt servicing and IMF-linked fiscal reforms constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese, Gulf, and Western financiers compete for influence over transport, energy, and digital infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Northern Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and Northern Corridor remain strategic gateways for regional trade, exposing Kenya to competition and pressure from neighboring states and external investors over logistics and security.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but reinforce asymmetric dependence and expose Maseru to disputes over pricing, delays, and project financing.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Industrial Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The export economy remains highly exposed to external market access, foreign-owned factories, and changing trade preferences, limiting domestic control over industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore and Gold Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects offer revenue and jobs but leave Liberia dependent on concession terms, logistics agreements, and external commodity prices. Weak oversight continues to complicate local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and surrounding infrastructure attract competing foreign investors, while financing needs give external partners leverage over strategic assets and procurement decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Split Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest oil fields, export terminals, and revenue allocation. Foreign-backed actors can disrupt production or use energy assets as bargaining tools.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, Egypt, the UAE, and European actors retain competing security and migration interests in Libya. Their involvement limits unified national control over territory and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining operations remain dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains. Fiscal benefits are significant but contested against environmental and sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Chronic power shortages and limited transport capacity increase reliance on external financiers and operators. Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western interests are competing for influence over ports, logistics, and strategic minerals.

highlights: Mining and Energy Seen as Exit Routes

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms are stabilizing the macroeconomic position, but creditors and donors retain substantial influence over fiscal and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects and persistent electricity shortages could provide capital and growth while limiting domestic control over strategic resources and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced Western influence but relies increasingly on Russian security assistance, creating asymmetric dependence and limited transparency over associated concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Nationalization Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking a larger share of gold revenues through revised rules and disputes with foreign operators, raising legal, operational, and investor-retaliation risks.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen Mauritania's fiscal and geopolitical leverage, but reliance on foreign operators and cross-border revenue arrangements limits unilateral control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and prospective green-energy projects depend heavily on foreign capital, logistics, and export infrastructure, leaving exposure to commodity cycles and external commercial priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation Risks
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty transition over the Chagos Archipelago remains strategically sensitive because security arrangements, base access, and implementation details involve the United Kingdom and the United States.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, digital, and maritime investments from India, China, and Western partners create opportunities for Mauritius but require careful balancing to preserve strategic autonomy.

highlights: Resource Diplomacy, Port and Energy Expansion

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contestation
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control claims and development strategy in Western Sahara continue to drive tensions with Algeria and the Polisario Front while complicating relations with external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Sectors
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen, critical minerals, phosphates, and port projects attract major foreign investment, but long-term concessions and supply-chain dependencies require continued state oversight.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and LNG Access
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in Cabo Delgado continues to shape the operating environment for international LNG developers and foreign security partners. Maputo risks retaining limited control over project security and revenue outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Revenue and Local Benefit-Sharing
frictionVectors.details: Large LNG projects remain dependent on external capital, technology, and export infrastructure. Disputes over delayed benefits, displacement, and revenue transparency could intensify local grievances.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Offshore Discoveries
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas prospects offer Namibia greater fiscal leverage but are led by international operators with advanced capital and technical capacity. The government must secure stronger local participation and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen Infrastructure and Water Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen plans depend on foreign finance, export corridors, and scarce water resources. Large projects could generate strategic infrastructure while limiting domestic value capture if supply chains remain externally controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while reducing Western influence. Weak administrative capacity and uncertain contracts could deter investment without guaranteeing stronger sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports depend on cross-border pipeline infrastructure and relations with coastal neighbors. Political isolation, insecurity, and disputes over transit arrangements leave the export chain exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline sabotage, theft, and illegal refining continue to reduce state and operator control over crude flows. Security reforms and community agreements have improved conditions unevenly but have not solved the structural problem.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital and Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is seeking foreign investment across gas, power, ports, and critical minerals while attempting to retain greater domestic value. Currency pressures, regulatory uncertainty, and infrastructure bottlenecks constrain that bargaining position.

highlights: Eastern Congo Ties Raise External Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Linked Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral trading is under sustained scrutiny because of allegations linking eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo conflict networks to mineral flows. Diplomatic pressure and traceability demands could affect export access and investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on External Finance
frictionVectors.details: The government maintains strong administrative control over strategic projects but remains reliant on foreign aid, concessional finance, and investment. External financing conditions can therefore limit policy autonomy despite effective domestic coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore blocks attract foreign operators, but limited discoveries and weak domestic capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe’s bargaining power. The government faces pressure to preserve maritime rights while avoiding unfavorable long-term concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Security
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and maritime crime threaten control over the country’s exclusive economic zone. São Tomé relies heavily on external naval cooperation and donor-funded surveillance.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is reviewing oil, gas, mining, and fisheries arrangements to increase national participation and transparency. Renegotiation risks legal disputes, investor caution, and delays to planned revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production and gas-to-power projects remain dependent on foreign technical, financial, and marketing partners. Dakar is seeking greater domestic processing and local-content benefits without disrupting project financing.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna and Maritime Access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and distant-water fishing agreements continue to test Seychelles’ control over marine resources. The country is using licensing, monitoring, and blue-bond mechanisms to capture more value while protecting stocks.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Security Partners
frictionVectors.details: India, France, China, and other partners seek maritime access and influence in the western Indian Ocean. Seychelles generally preserves autonomy through diversified partnerships, but port and surveillance cooperation requires careful balancing.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore and Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and fiscal expectations, leaving the government exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over royalties and local benefits. Limited domestic processing reduces sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and mining infrastructure can improve connectivity but may lock the state into asymmetrical commercial arrangements. Freetown faces pressure to secure transparent financing and stronger local-content obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Naval and Port Access
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, the United States, and other partners provide security, training, and infrastructure support, but their competing access interests complicate unified federal control. Port agreements and maritime cooperation remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Potential oil and gas development is constrained by federal-state disputes, insecurity, and limited regulatory capacity. Without a credible revenue-sharing and licensing framework, foreign exploration could deepen internal tensions rather than strengthen national sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port congestion constrain domestic control over mineral value chains. Foreign capital remains important for generation, mining, and logistics modernization.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group minerals, creating leverage but also pressure over export policy and local beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on a vulnerable pipeline route through Sudan and external operators to monetize its principal resource. Conflict damage, transit disputes, and opaque revenue management sharply limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Political stabilization relies heavily on neighboring states, international donors, and peacekeeping support. Elite competition and localized violence continue to threaten infrastructure and agricultural recovery.

highlights: Gold and ports attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Externalized gold economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed networks and foreign intermediaries shape gold production and export routes, diverting revenue from state institutions. Regional and Gulf-linked interests add layers of geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime facilities, and aid corridors are strategic assets contested amid the civil war. Outside powers are seeking influence while military disruption undermines national control of trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns from gold, nickel, graphite, and other minerals while balancing investment from Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked firms.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and LNG leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and natural-gas projects increase strategic autonomy but create dependence on external financiers, contractors, and export markets. Dar es Salaam's regional-corridor role is becoming more geopolitically valuable.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to national revenue and Sahel trade, but its performance depends on foreign shipping, logistics, and financing networks. Regional instability can disrupt transit flows and increase external bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from Burkina Faso threatens northern communities and transport links, drawing Togo into deeper security cooperation with regional and extra-regional partners.

highlights: Phosphate and energy sovereignty under pressure
Europe remains the decisive economic interlocutor

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding, trade access, and migration cooperation give the EU substantial influence over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress limits Tunis's bargaining room with external creditors and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported gas and electricity exposes Tunisia to external price and supply shocks. Renewable-energy projects could improve autonomy but remain reliant on foreign capital and technology.

highlights: Oil development tied to Tanzania corridor

frictionVectors.title: East African Crude Oil Pipeline
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's export strategy depends on the Tanzania pipeline, creating exposure to partner-state politics, financing constraints, and international environmental opposition. The project remains central to Kampala's resource-sovereignty agenda.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked contractors and lenders retain a major role in roads, energy, and industrial projects. Debt-service pressure could narrow Uganda's room to negotiate contracts and manage future oil revenues.

highlights: Debt restructuring opens new bargaining space

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors compete for influence over mines, smelters, and logistics. Zambia is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns, but remains exposed to external capital and commodity pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito and regional corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor offers an alternative to routes dominated by southern and eastern African networks, but its development will bring competing foreign interests in rail, minerals, and port access.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply involved in lithium and other mineral projects, while Western and regional actors seek alternative access. Zimbabwe's push for domestic beneficiation is constrained by financing, technology, and sanctions-related restrictions.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and infrastructure fragility
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages and aging infrastructure limit mineral processing and broader industrial capacity. Reliance on imports, regional power pools, and external infrastructure finance weakens effective control over resource development.
